stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many museums digitize their print collections with flatbed scanners. These scanners reproduce ink color accurately, but they light each sheet evenly from directly above, so the faint ridges a press leaves in damp paper nearly disappear. When cataloguing a museum's Japanese woodblock prints, conservator Mariko Ishida instead photographed each sheet under light cast at a low angle across its surface, a technique that throws those ridges into sharp shadow. Ishida's choice suggests that she regarded ______
choices: low-angle lighting as a way to reproduce a print's ink colors more accurately than flatbed scanning does.
the texture pressed into a print's paper as information that a flatbed scan would fail to preserve.
the ink colors of the prints as more historically significant than the marks left in the paper by the press.
flatbed scanners as unsuitable for recording any feature of a print, including the colors of its ink.
explanation: Ask why Ishida would drop the standard method. The passage gives only one flaw of flatbed scanning: it hides the ridges a press leaves in the paper. Her replacement method is the one that reveals those ridges. So she must have thought that texture was worth recording and that a flatbed scan would lose it.

A.why: You gave Ishida a belief her choice never needed. The passage says flatbed scanners already reproduce color accurately, and it presents low-angle light as a way to show the ridges, not as a way to improve color.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Ishida picked a method designed to capture the press marks, so she can't have thought those marks mattered less than the ink colors that flatbed scans already handle well.

D.why: You went too far. Ishida only needed to think flatbed scans are limited, since they miss the texture. The passage itself says they record ink color accurately, so 'any feature' claims much more than her choice supports.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: A regional health department has long estimated the spread of norovirus by tallying cases reported by local clinics. In 2023, while continuing to collect those clinic reports, the department also began testing samples of municipal wastewater for the virus's genetic material, which infected people shed whether or not they ever seek medical care. This decision suggests that department officials believed ______
choices: clinic reports had become so unreliable that they no longer offered any useful information about norovirus.
norovirus was spreading more rapidly through the region in 2023 than it had in any earlier year.
clinic reports, though still worth gathering, missed infections among people who never visited a clinic.
wastewater testing would detect norovirus infections in the region less completely than clinic reports had.
explanation: This takes two steps. First, the department added a method that picks up infections in people who never seek care, so officials must have thought clinic counts were missing those people. Second, the department kept collecting clinic reports, so officials still considered them worth having. Only this choice includes both parts: the reports are limited, but they aren't worthless.

A.why: You treated 'limited' as 'useless.' The department kept collecting clinic reports, which shows officials still valued them. They only thought the reports were incomplete.

B.why: You assigned a belief the decision doesn't depend on. Wastewater testing makes sense because clinic counts miss some cases, not because of a rise in infections. The passage never mentions how fast norovirus was spreading.

D.why: You reversed the comparison. Wastewater testing was added because it captures infections that clinic reports miss, so officials must have expected it to be more complete, not less.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Linguists documenting little-studied languages often rely on elicitation, asking a speaker to translate prepared sentences from a widely spoken language such as Spanish. Some researchers worry that the method nudges speakers toward the word order of the original sentence. In documenting a Zapotec variety spoken in southern Mexico, linguist Tomás Uribe instead recorded several hundred hours of unscripted conversation among speakers and transcribed it afterward. Uribe's approach suggests that, in Uribe's view, ______
choices: translations of prepared sentences may show features of Spanish rather than of the variety being documented.
translations of prepared sentences always misrepresent the grammar of the variety being documented.
unscripted conversation is less likely than translation to reflect how speakers ordinarily talk.
speakers of the variety are generally unwilling to translate sentences prepared by outside researchers.
explanation: The passage names one specific worry about elicitation: the source sentence can pull the speaker toward its word order. Uribe avoided elicitation entirely and recorded natural speech, so Uribe must have shared at least some of that concern. Choosing a different method shows only that Uribe thought the problem could happen, which matches the hedge 'may.'

B.why: You fell for strength creep. Researchers only 'worry' that elicitation nudges speakers. Avoiding a risk shows Uribe took that risk seriously, not that Uribe thought elicitation 'always' gets the grammar wrong. Circle words like 'always' before you commit.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Uribe recorded conversation specifically to avoid the distortion that translation can introduce, so Uribe must have thought conversation was the more natural evidence.

D.why: You assigned a belief the approach never needed. The passage explains Uribe's choice through a concern about distorted data, not through any reluctance on the speakers' part.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Most studies of minimum-wage increases measure their effect by counting how many people are employed before and after the change. When economist Leila Haddad examined a 2022 minimum-wage increase in several Canadian provinces, Haddad counted employees as well but also tracked the average number of hours each employee worked per week. This design suggests that Haddad thought ______
choices: employers would certainly respond to the increase by trimming workers' hours rather than by reducing staff.
counts of employed people reveal nothing useful about how a minimum-wage increase affects workers.
changes in weekly hours are a less sensitive measure of an increase's effects than changes in headcount.
employers might respond to the increase by trimming workers' hours rather than by reducing their staff.
explanation: Ask why Haddad would add a measure of hours. Headcount alone can't detect a change in which everyone keeps their job but works less. Tracking hours makes sense only if Haddad thought that kind of response was possible. Possible is all the design shows, so 'might' is as strong as the answer can go.

A.why: You let the modal creep upward. Researchers measure something to find out whether it happens. Tracking hours shows Haddad thought cuts were possible, not that they would 'certainly' occur.

B.why: You treated a limited tool as a useless one. Haddad still counted employees and only added hours alongside that count, so Haddad clearly thought headcounts were informative.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. Haddad added hours because they can reveal effects that headcount misses, so Haddad must have seen hours as able to catch more, not less.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: City traffic engineers have traditionally graded streets using "level of service," a score based on how long drivers wait at intersections. In a 2021 report, urban planner Aisha Okonkwo-Reyes recommended that her city keep this score but also grade each street on how many people it moves per hour, counting those who travel on foot, by bicycle, and by bus along with those in cars. Okonkwo-Reyes's recommendation implies that she considered ______
choices: drivers' waiting times at intersections to be irrelevant to judging how well a city street works.
a grade based only on drivers' waiting times to give an incomplete account of how well a street works.
the existing grade to capture travel on foot and by bus more fully than the proposed measure would.
the streets that move the most people per hour to be the ones where drivers wait the longest.
explanation: If someone recommends adding a measure, they think the current one leaves something out. The existing score counts only drivers' delays, and the proposed measure adds walkers, cyclists, and bus riders, so Okonkwo-Reyes must have thought a driver-only score misses part of how well a street serves people. She kept the old score, so 'incomplete' is the right strength.

A.why: You treated a limited measure as a worthless one. She recommended keeping the level-of-service score, so she can't have thought drivers' waiting times were irrelevant.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. The existing score is based on drivers' waiting times, and the new measure was proposed so that walkers and bus riders would be counted. She must have thought the new measure captures them better.

D.why: You assigned a belief the recommendation never needed. Her proposal only requires thinking that a driver-only score leaves people out. It says nothing about any link between how many people a street moves and how long drivers wait.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many growers decide when to irrigate by checking a single moisture sensor buried a few centimeters below the soil surface. Agronomist Lucía Ferraz, however, has urged growers of deep-rooted crops such as alfalfa to add sensors at depths of 60 and 90 centimeters, even though doing so roughly triples the cost of monitoring a field. Ferraz's recommendation suggests that in her view, ______
choices: surface sensors are so unreliable that growers should stop using them altogether.
the cost of extra sensors is the main reason growers have not adopted them.
surface readings alone can misrepresent the water available to deep roots.
deep-rooted crops need less frequent irrigation than shallow-rooted crops do.
explanation: Ask why Ferraz would add deeper sensors and accept triple the cost. That only makes sense if she thinks the single shallow sensor leaves something out: it can't show how much water there is down where alfalfa roots grow. So her recommendation depends on the belief that surface readings alone can misrepresent the water available to deep roots.

A.why: You pushed 'limited' into 'useless.' Ferraz adds sensors alongside the surface sensor and doesn't replace it, so she only needs to think the surface reading is incomplete, not unreliable.

B.why: You picked up on the cost detail. The passage says she recommends the sensors despite the cost. It never says she thinks cost explains why growers haven't adopted them, and her recommendation doesn't depend on that belief.

D.why: You credited Ferraz with a belief her recommendation never needs. She makes no comparison of irrigation frequency between crop types. Her point is about where to measure moisture.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: For decades, a regional weather office published a single predicted snowfall total before each winter storm. When staff reviewed ten years of these forecasts, they found that actual totals often differed sharply from predictions for storms tracking near the rain-snow line, where small temperature shifts decide whether precipitation falls as rain or snow. The office now issues a range of likely totals for such storms but keeps single totals for storms well inland. This change suggests the staff believed that ______
choices: single totals had been inaccurate for every type of storm the office forecast.
storms well inland were harder to forecast than storms near the rain-snow line.
storms near the rain-snow line had become more frequent over the past decade.
a single total implied more certainty than storms near the rain-snow line allowed.
explanation: The office switched to ranges only for storms near the rain-snow line, which are the storms where its review found large misses. That choice depends on the belief that a single number made those forecasts look more certain than they could be. Keeping single totals for inland storms shows the staff didn't have the same doubt about those storms.

A.why: You stretched one problem to cover every storm. The office kept single totals for inland storms, so the staff can't have thought those totals were inaccurate.

B.why: You reversed the comparison. The office treats storms near the rain-snow line as the harder case. That's why only those storms now get a range.

C.why: You credited the staff with a belief the change doesn't need. The review was about forecast accuracy, not how often these storms happen, and nothing suggests their frequency changed.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Most clinics in Harlow County remind patients about overdue vaccinations by sending a mailed postcard, a practice that has gone largely unchanged for years. The county health department has now funded a six-month trial in which half of the clinics switch to text-message reminders while the other half continue mailing postcards. By funding this trial, the department indicates that in its view, ______
choices: postcards have already been shown to work less well than text messages.
mailed postcards may not be the most effective reminder clinics could use.
text-message reminders would cost clinics more to send than postcards.
all clinics should stop mailing postcards before the trial has concluded.
explanation: Nobody pays for a head-to-head trial of an old method against a new one unless they think the old method might not be the best option. The trial is meant to find out, so the department's belief can only be that postcards may not be the most effective reminder. It can't be that postcards are known to be worse.

A.why: You turned 'might be' into 'has been shown.' If the comparison were already settled, there would be no reason to run the trial. The department suspects something; it hasn't proven it.

C.why: You credited the department with a belief the trial never depends on. The passage says nothing about cost, and funding the trial doesn't require any view about which method is cheaper.

D.why: You missed the trial's design. Half the clinics keep mailing postcards so there's something to compare against. Stopping postcards everywhere would wreck the trial the department is funding.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Surveys of marsh birds have traditionally relied on observers who stand at fixed points and record every bird they see or hear. Ornithologist Dev Rao notes, however, that secretive species such as rails rarely call when people are close by. For his survey of a Louisiana marsh, Rao placed automated recorders at the usual survey points and left them unattended overnight. Rao's approach suggests that he thought ______
choices: rails call more often when observers are present than when they are absent.
automated recorders detect every marsh species more accurately than people do.
marsh birds are more numerous at night than they are during the day.
the presence of observers can cause some species to be undercounted.
explanation: Rao points to one problem: rails go quiet when people are nearby. He then takes the people out and leaves recorders. That only makes sense if he thinks a human observer can reduce how many of these birds are detected. In other words, the observer's presence can lead to some species being undercounted.

A.why: You reversed the relationship. The passage says rails rarely call when people are close. Calling more when observers are present is the opposite of the problem Rao is trying to solve.

B.why: You let 'some species' grow into 'every species.' Rao's reasoning is about secretive birds like rails. Nothing suggests he thinks recorders do better for all birds.

C.why: You read too much into the word 'overnight.' Leaving the recorders unattended takes people away from the birds. It doesn't require Rao to believe bird numbers change between day and night.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Folklorists have often assumed that a tale found in many villages spread outward from one original version, and they have arranged variants into family trees tracing each back to that source. In cataloging 140 versions of a Baltic tale about a bargaining fox, however, Ilse Varga built no such tree. She grouped the versions by region and by the occasions on which they were told. Varga's choice suggests that she ______
choices: considered the regional versions too alike to be worth telling apart.
believed the tale was first told in a single village that could be identified.
questioned whether descent from one source was a sound way to organize them.
regarded earlier folklorists' catalogs as containing no useful information.
explanation: The passage sets up the usual method, which is a family tree going back to one source, and then says Varga set it aside on purpose. A scholar drops the standard approach and organizes by region and occasion when she doubts the standard approach fits the material. So her choice suggests she questioned whether descent from one original was a sound way to organize the versions.

A.why: You missed what her grouping implies. Sorting the versions by region only makes sense if she thinks regional differences are worth showing. That's the opposite of finding the versions too alike.

B.why: You attributed the old view to the person who turned away from it. Believing in one identifiable source village is the assumption behind the family tree she chose not to build.

D.why: You turned a difference in method into a total rejection. Varga declined one way of organizing the material. That doesn't mean she thinks earlier catalogs are worthless.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Vaccine protection is commonly judged by the level of antibodies in the blood, and those levels typically fall in the months after a dose. Immunologist Rana Okafor, however, recruited volunteers whose antibody levels had already dropped below the threshold usually treated as protective, then tested whether their memory T cells still responded to the virus. Okafor's choice of participants suggests that in Okafor's view, ______
choices: a drop in antibody levels does not necessarily mean that a person's protection has been lost.
memory T cells, rather than antibodies, are the only source of lasting protection against the virus.
antibody levels are a more dependable measure of protection than memory T-cell responses are.
vaccine doses should be given more often so that antibody levels stay above the usual threshold.
explanation: Ask why Okafor would deliberately study people whose antibodies had fallen below the protective threshold. That study only makes sense if Okafor suspected those people might still be protected in another way, through memory T cells. So Okafor must doubt that low antibodies alone mean protection is gone. Choice A states that assumption and nothing more.

B.why: You went from 'antibodies may not tell the whole story' to 'T cells are the ONLY source of protection.' Okafor's study requires only that T cells might add something, not that antibodies contribute nothing. Watch for 'only.'

C.why: This reverses the comparison. Okafor looked past antibody levels to T cells, which suggests Okafor thinks antibody levels miss something. That is the opposite of trusting them more.

D.why: This assumes Okafor treats the antibody threshold as the thing that matters. The study questions that threshold, and nothing in the passage is about dosing schedules.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many nineteenth-century folktale collections were assembled by editors who rewrote what they heard into polished literary prose, trimming repetitions and replacing regional expressions with standard ones. Folklorist Tomas Ilves has urged scholars who trace how particular tales shifted from one generation of tellers to the next to rely instead on audio recordings of storytellers made since the 1930s. Ilves's recommendation implies that, in Ilves's view, ______
choices: printed nineteenth-century collections have no value for any kind of folklore research.
nineteenth-century editors preserved tellers' exact wording more closely than recordings do.
editorial rewriting in the printed collections hides details needed to track how tales changed.
storytellers recorded since the 1930s performed tales more skillfully than earlier tellers did.
explanation: Ilves recommends recordings for one task: tracing how tales shifted between generations. The passage names the flaw in the printed collections. Editors smoothed away repetitions and regional wording, and those small variations are exactly what you would compare across generations. The recommendation therefore depends on the belief that the rewriting hides those details, which is what choice C says.

A.why: Ilves's advice applies to one research question. Thinking the collections are limited for that purpose is not the same as thinking they are useless for 'any kind' of research. The trap here is strength creep.

B.why: This reverses the comparison. The passage says editors changed tellers' wording, and Ilves prefers recordings for that reason. Ilves can't believe the printed versions are more faithful.

D.why: Ilves cares about how accurately a performance was captured, not how good it was. The recommendation doesn't depend on any view of the tellers' skill.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Ecologists have long surveyed forest birds using point counts, in which an observer stands at a fixed spot and records every bird seen or heard. Because most birds in dense forest are detected by their calls, such counts tend to miss species that seldom vocalize. In a recent survey of a cloud forest, ecologist Mei Tanaka supplemented point counts with motion-triggered cameras mounted near the forest floor. Tanaka's approach suggests that Tanaka thought ______
choices: point counts give inaccurate results for every bird species that lives in cloud forests.
the forest might hold quiet ground-dwelling birds that point counts alone would undercount.
ground-dwelling birds in cloud forests call more often than birds in the canopy do.
cloud forests support more bird species than any other type of forest habitat does.
explanation: The passage states the flaw in point counts: they miss birds that rarely call. Tanaka added cameras, which detect birds by movement rather than sound, and placed them near the ground. That choice only makes sense if Tanaka expected some quiet birds on or near the forest floor that the counts would miss. Choice B states that belief.

A.why: Tanaka kept the point counts and supplemented them. That shows Tanaka thinks they fall short for some species, not that they fail for 'every' species. Look for the word that goes too far.

C.why: This is backward. Cameras near the ground are useful because they catch birds that rarely call. If ground birds called often, the point counts would already find them.

D.why: Tanaka's approach is about how to detect birds, not how many species cloud forests have compared with other forests. The approach doesn't depend on that comparison.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Aluminum ship hulls are commonly protected with chromate coatings, which resist corrosion well but release toxic compounds into the water as they wear. Materials engineer Priya Venkataraman spent three years developing a cerium-based alternative. In her latest trial, she submerged panels in seawater for eighteen months. The cerium coating protected slightly less well than chromate, by a margin she called "acceptable for most hull applications." Venkataraman's recommendation that shipyards adopt the cerium coating suggests that she believes ______
choices: the cerium coating resists seawater corrosion more effectively than chromate does.
the environmental benefit of the cerium coating outweighs its small shortfall in protection.
chromate coatings offer too little corrosion protection to be worth applying to hulls.
the cerium coating is suitable for all hull applications now using chromate, without exception.
explanation: Ask why she would recommend a coating that she found protects slightly less well. She must think its advantage, not releasing chromate's toxic compounds, is worth more than the small loss in protection. Choice B states exactly the belief her recommendation depends on.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. The trial found that the cerium coating protected slightly *less* well than chromate, not better.

C.why: You went too far. The passage says chromate resists corrosion well. Venkataraman objects to its toxicity, not its protection, so she never needs to think it is worthless.

D.why: You missed the quantifier. She called the margin acceptable for *most* hull applications. Saying all of them, without exception, claims more than she does.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many forest managers blame the poor survival of oak seedlings in eastern North America chiefly on browsing by white-tailed deer, and fencing is the standard remedy. When ecologist Tomás Ibarra designed a study of oak regeneration, however, he did not simply compare fenced plots with unfenced ones. Within each group, he also thinned the overhead canopy on half the plots, letting more sunlight reach the forest floor. Ibarra's design suggests that he suspected ______
choices: deer browsing has little or no effect on whether oak seedlings survive.
shade could account for part of the seedling loss usually blamed on deer.
seedlings survive better beneath a dense canopy than beneath a thinned one.
shade causes far more seedling loss among oaks than deer browsing does.
explanation: Ibarra kept the deer comparison and added a light comparison. A researcher tests canopy thinning only if they think light might also matter. So he suspected that shade explains at least some of the loss that managers attribute to deer. Choice B claims only that much.

A.why: You went too far. Ibarra still fenced half his plots, so he was testing deer too. Nothing shows he thought deer don't matter.

C.why: You reversed the comparison. He thinned the canopy to let in more light, which only makes sense if he suspected more light might *help* seedlings survive.

D.why: You turned a suspicion into a ranking. Testing both factors shows he thought shade might matter. It doesn't show he expected shade to outweigh deer, let alone by a wide margin.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Forecasters estimate hail size largely from radar, which measures how strongly a storm reflects microwave signals high in the atmosphere. Hailstones, however, can melt substantially as they fall through warm air near the ground. After reviewing a season of storms in which radar estimates and ground reports differed, meteorologist Ama Owusu recommended that her agency recruit volunteers to measure hailstones on the ground in low-lying, warmer regions. Owusu's recommendation implies that she believes ______
choices: radar tends to overestimate the size of hail reaching the ground in warm areas.
radar tends to underestimate the size of hail reaching the ground in warm areas.
radar estimates of hail size are unreliable in every region the agency covers.
melting hail adds significantly to rainfall totals in low-lying, warmer regions.
explanation: Radar measures hail high in the storm, and hail shrinks as it melts in warm air near the ground. Owusu asks for ground measurements specifically in warm, low-lying places. That choice only makes sense if she thinks the hail that lands there is smaller than radar indicates, meaning radar overestimates it. Choice A states this.

B.why: You reversed the direction of the gap. Melting makes hailstones smaller on the way down, so radar would read them as larger than they are when they land, not smaller.

C.why: You missed the limit she set. She asked for volunteers only in low-lying, warmer regions, which suggests she trusts radar elsewhere. 'Every region' claims more than her recommendation shows.

D.why: You picked up an incidental detail. Melting is mentioned to explain why hail size changes, not to make a point about rainfall. Her recommendation is about measuring hail size, and this choice never touches that.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: For decades, a regional weather office based its fog warnings on readings from a single station at the county airport. In 2023, forecaster Lena Ortiz recommended adding a network of low-cost visibility sensors along the river valley. She noted that fog in the valley often forms hours before it drifts toward the airport. Ortiz's recommendation suggests that she did NOT believe that ______
choices: fog conditions in the valley can differ from conditions measured at the airport.
the airport station's readings were enough on their own to warn valley residents.
detecting valley fog earlier would help the office issue more timely warnings.
inexpensive sensors could supply visibility readings useful to forecasters.
explanation: Ask why Ortiz would recommend new sensors at all. Her recommendation only makes sense if she thought the single airport station fell short, since fog forms in the valley hours before it reaches the airport. So she did NOT believe the airport readings were enough on their own. The other three choices are all things she had to believe for her recommendation to make sense. The blank asks for the one she rejected.

A.why: This is the belief her whole recommendation rests on. She says valley fog forms before it reaches the airport, so she clearly thinks the two locations can differ. You found a true statement about her view and missed the NOT in the blank.

C.why: She points out that the fog forms 'hours before' it reaches the airport, and that point only matters if catching it earlier helps. She held this belief, so it can't be the one she did NOT hold.

D.why: You latched onto the detail that the sensors are cheap and read it as a doubt about their quality. Nobody recommends a sensor network they think will give useless readings, so she did believe this.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many conservation groups judge the health of a seabird colony by counting its nesting pairs each spring. Ecologist Tomás Reyna's team, however, spent three seasons also weighing chicks just before they fledged. The researchers argued that a colony can hold its nest count steady even as food shortages leave young birds too light to survive their first winter. The team's approach suggests that the researchers did NOT assume that ______
choices: a chick's weight at fledging can affect its chances of surviving the winter.
the food available to a colony can influence how its chicks develop.
a colony's health can decline without any change in its nest count.
a steady number of nesting pairs reliably shows that a colony is thriving.
explanation: The passage opens with the popular method of counting nests and then undercuts it. Reyna's team added chick weights because they believed nest counts can stay level while the colony is in trouble. A team with that view could not assume that a steady nest count reliably shows a thriving colony. The other three choices are assumptions the team needed to justify weighing chicks.

A.why: The team says chicks can be 'too light to survive their first winter', which is exactly this belief. You picked a statement the researchers did hold and overlooked the NOT.

B.why: The researchers name food shortages as the reason chicks end up too light, so they clearly believed food affects how chicks develop. This assumption supports their method. It is not one they rejected.

C.why: This is the researchers' central argument, nearly word for word. You may have read it as the 'corrected view' and picked it, but the blank asks for the view they did NOT hold.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Hikers in the Vellan Range have long relied on a 1960s survey map with contour lines spaced at 50-meter intervals. When the park service commissioned a replacement, cartographer Ines Halvorsen insisted on 10-meter contours for the steep eastern trails. On the gentle western plateau, however, she kept the original 50-meter spacing. Halvorsen's decision implies that she did NOT think that ______
choices: 50-meter contours were too coarse for every part of the range.
finer contours would reveal detail that matters on the eastern trails.
50-meter contours were adequate for mapping the western plateau.
the old map's spacing hid terrain features that matter on some trails.
explanation: Halvorsen changed the spacing in one place and kept it in another. That split tells you she thought the old 50-meter contours were limited, not useless. She kept them for the western plateau, so she could not have thought they were too coarse for every part of the range. This choice goes too far, and that is why it is the belief she did NOT hold.

B.why: She insisted on 10-meter contours for the eastern trails, and that only makes sense if she thought the finer spacing showed detail that mattered there. She held this belief.

C.why: She deliberately kept the 50-meter spacing on the plateau, which shows she thought it was good enough there. You may have assumed a new map rejects everything about the old one, but the passage says otherwise.

D.why: Replacing the eastern contours implies she thought the old spacing hid something that mattered there. The word 'some' keeps this claim modest enough to match her view, so it is a belief she held.
